questions.q: Name the two main vascular tissues in plants and state the primary substance each transports. Also, specify the direction of transport in each.
questions.a: Xylem transports water and minerals upward (unidirectional, root to shoot). Phloem transports food (mainly sucrose) bidirectionally (source to sink). A wrong answer (e.g., "xylem transports food" or "phloem transports water upward only") reveals confusion between the two transport systems and ignorance of directionality — a common 1-mark board exam error.

questions.q: Explain why xylem transport is described as a 'passive process' while phloem transport requires 'living companion cells'. What would happen to phloem transport if companion cells were killed by a metabolic inhibitor?
questions.a: Xylem uses dead vessels/tracheids; water moves by physical forces (transpiration pull, cohesion, adhesion) without metabolic energy. Phloem loading of sucrose into sieve tubes requires ATP-driven active transport by living companion cells; killing them stops loading, collapsing the osmotic gradient, and halting translocation. A wrong answer (e.g., "both need energy" or "xylem uses root pressure only") shows misunderstanding of energy sources — a frequent 2-mark board question trap.

questions.q: A student ties a plastic bag around a leafy branch of a mango tree in the afternoon. After 2 hours, water droplets collect inside the bag. Identify the process, name the driving force, and state two environmental factors that would increase the rate of this process.
questions.a: Process: Transpiration (specifically stomatal transpiration). Driving force: Transpiration pull (cohesion-tension) created by evaporation from stomata. Factors increasing rate: (1) High temperature, (2) Low humidity / wind speed. A wrong answer confusing this with guttation (which occurs at night, high humidity, root pressure) or naming photosynthesis as the driver reveals a critical confusion between transpiration and guttation — a classic board exam case-study error.

questions.q: Compare the mechanism of water movement in xylem (cohesion-tension theory) with food movement in phloem (pressure-flow hypothesis) in a table with columns: Driving Force, Role of Living Cells, Direction, Energy Requirement, Evidence (one experiment each).
questions.a:
| Aspect | Xylem (Cohesion-Tension) | Phloem (Pressure-Flow) |
|--------|--------------------------|------------------------|
| Driving Force | Transpiration pull (negative pressure/tension) | Osmotic pressure gradient (positive pressure) |
| Living Cells | Not required (vessels/tracheids dead) | Essential (companion cells load/unload sucrose) |
| Direction | Unidirectional (upward) | Bidirectional (source to sink) |
| Energy | Passive (solar energy drives evaporation) | Active loading/unloading (ATP from companion cells) |
| Key Experiment | Transpiration pull shown by suction in cut stem / potometer | Girdling/ringing experiment (phloem removed → swelling above cut) |

A wrong table swapping driving forces or claiming xylem needs ATP shows failure to analyze the fundamental physical vs. physiological distinction — a 3-5 mark board question.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Root pressure is the main force pushing water up tall trees like Eucalyptus (height > 50 m)." Justify your answer with two pieces of evidence from plant physiology.
questions.a: Statement is FALSE. Evidence: (1) Root pressure can only push water up a few meters (max ~10-20 m) — insufficient for tall trees. (2) Transpiration pull (cohesion-tension) operates continuously during day and can lift water >100 m due to water's high tensile strength from cohesion-adhesion. Root pressure mainly causes guttation at night in small herbs. A student agreeing reveals over-reliance on root pressure and ignorance of cohesion-tension theory's dominance — a conceptual error costing marks in assertion-reason questions.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a potted plant, oil, and a weighing balance to prove that most water absorbed by roots is lost by transpiration, not used in growth. List materials, steps, control, observation, and conclusion.
questions.a: Materials: Potted plant, water, oil layer (to prevent soil evaporation), weighing balance, polythene bag (to cover soil). Steps: (1) Water plant, cover soil with oil + bag. (2) Weigh initial mass. (3) Keep in sunlight for 4 hours. (4) Weigh final mass. Control: Identical setup without plant (or with dead plant) to account for pot evaporation. Observation: Significant mass loss only in live plant. Conclusion: Mass loss = water transpired; growth uses <5% of absorbed water. A poor design missing the oil layer or control shows inability to isolate variables — a practical-based board exam skill gap.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Transportation in plants is the vital biological process by which water, minerals, and synthesized food (mainly sucrose) are moved through specialized vascular tissues: xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals ______ from roots to aerial parts via transpiration pull, while phloem translocates photosynthates bidirectionally from source (photosynthetic leaves) to sink (roots, fruits, growing tissues) through the pressure-flow mechanism.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a tall coconut tree in Kerala drawing water from deep sandy soil up to its crown 20 ______ high without a pump — how does it defy gravity?
What is Transportation in plants? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Transportation in plants is the vital biological process by which water, minerals, and synthesized food (mainly sucrose) are moved through specialized vascular tissues: xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals unidirectionally from roots to aerial parts via transpiration pull, while phloem translocates photosynthates bidirectionally.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine a tall coconut tree in Kerala drawing water from deep sandy soil up to its crown ______ meters high without a pump — how does it defy gravity?
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Transportation in plants?
questions.a: Students believe "phloem transports food only downward from leaves to roots" because textbooks often show arrows downward.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain the mechanism of water ascent in xylem using cohesion-tension-transpiration pull theory with correct terminology (adhesion, cohesion, transpiration pull, root pressure) and describe phloem translocation via pressure-flow hypothesis, including the roles of sieve tubes, companion cells, loading/unloading of sucrose.
